summary: At a supper in Bethany, Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus. Judas and others call it waste, but Jesus defends her and calls it an anointing for His burial.
key_insight: Judas and the others priced the perfume: three hundred denarii, nearly a year’s wages. Jesus did not argue the price. He spoke of time: “Me you do not have always.” The moment for this gift would last days, not years, and Mary did not let it pass.
story: In Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, {Mk} friends made Jesus a supper. Martha served, and Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead, was one of those at the table with Him. {Jn}

Then Mary took a pound of very costly oil of spikenard, {Jn} kept in an alabaster flask. She broke the flask and poured the oil on His head, {Mk} and she anointed His feet and wiped them with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the oil. {Jn}

Judas Iscariot, the disciple who would betray Him, objected: “Why was this fragrant oil not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” He said it not because he cared for the poor, but because he was a thief. He kept the money box and used to take what was put in it. {Jn} Others took up the complaint, “Why this waste?” {Mt} and they criticized her sharply. {Mk}

But Jesus said, “Let her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a good work for Me.” They would have the poor with them always, and could do them good whenever they wished, “but Me you do not have always. She has done what she could. She has come beforehand to anoint My body for burial.” {Mk}
“Assuredly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told as a memorial to her.”

Word spread that Jesus was there, and a great many people came out, not for His sake only, but to see Lazarus too. So the chief priests plotted to put Lazarus to death also, because on his account many were leaving them and believing in Jesus. {Jn}
differences: John sets the supper after Jesus came to Bethany “six days before the Passover,” on the evening before the Triumphal Entry. Matthew and Mark tell it later in their story, after noting that the Passover was two days away, and give the supper no date of its own.
Matthew and Mark say she poured the oil on His head; John says she anointed His feet and wiped them with her hair.
Only John names Mary, Martha and Lazarus, and says Judas raised the objection. Matthew says “His disciples” were indignant; Mark says “some.”
Mark and John give the price, three hundred denarii. Only Mark says she broke the flask and records “She has done what she could.”
Matthew and Mark name the house of Simon the leper and record Jesus’ promise of a memorial; only John tells of the plot to kill Lazarus.

fit.question: John places the anointing just after Jesus reached Bethany six days before Passover, on the night before the Triumphal Entry. Matthew and Mark tell it after saying Passover was two days away. When did it happen?

points.label: John gives the date
points.text: John ties the supper to a clear timeline: “six days before the Passover” (12:1), then “the next day” the entry (12:12). Matthew and Mark give the supper itself no date. Mark begins simply, “And being in Bethany” (14:3).

points.label: Placed beside the plot
points.text: Matthew and Mark set the supper between the leaders’ plot (Mark 14:1–2) and Judas’s visit to the chief priests (14:10–11). Told there, it shows what lay behind Judas’s move: a rebuke over money, then an offer to sell Jesus for money. Ancient writers often grouped events by connection rather than by date. McGarvey and most harmonies follow John’s timing.

fit.note: Matthew and Mark never claim the supper took place two days before Passover; they place it where it explains Judas. John supplies the date.
fit.short: John ties it to Jesus’ arrival six days before Passover. Matthew and Mark place the undated supper beside Judas’s bargain, which it helps explain.

fit.question: Did Mary anoint Jesus’ head (Matthew, Mark) or His feet (John)? And who complained: Judas (John), the disciples (Matthew) or “some” (Mark)?

points.label: Head and feet
points.text: A pound of nard was a large amount, nearly twelve ounces. Mary could pour it on His head and still anoint His feet. Matthew and Mark tell of the head, the honor given to a king or a guest; John tells of the feet and her hair, the humble side of the same act. Jesus’ own words cover both: “pouring this fragrant oil on My body” (Matthew 26:12).

points.label: One voice, then many
points.text: Judas spoke first, and others joined in. John, writing later, names the man who started it and exposes his motive. Matthew and Mark report the wider grumbling around the table.

fit.note: Each writer tells the part he chose to stress. Together they give a fuller picture, and nothing requires an error.
fit.short: She anointed both head and feet. Judas started the complaint and other disciples joined in.

scene.label: Spikenard
scene.text: Nard was a perfumed oil made from a plant that grows in the Himalayan mountains, so it came to Israel over long trade routes. It was sealed in flasks of alabaster, a soft, polished stone. Breaking the flask, as Mark says she did, suggests she meant to use all of it at once.

scene.label: Three hundred denarii
scene.text: A laborer earned about a denarius a day (Matthew 20:2). Three hundred denarii was close to a year’s wages, counting six working days a week. Judas and the others did the arithmetic at once.

scene.label: Simon the leper
scene.text: No one with active leprosy could host a meal, so Simon was probably a man Jesus had healed, still known by his old name. The Gospels do not say how he was related to Martha, Mary and Lazarus, though Martha’s serving suggests the families were close.

scene.label: The poor always
scene.text: Jesus’ words echo Deuteronomy 15:11: “For the poor will never cease from the land.” The same verse commands Israel to open its hand wide to the poor. Jesus was not dismissing the poor; gifts to the poor were customary at Passover, and the disciples later assumed Judas had gone out to make one (John 13:29).

scene.label: Anointed beforehand
scene.text: Bodies were prepared for burial with spices and oils (John 19:39–40). Jesus would be buried in haste on Friday evening, and the women who came on Sunday with spices “that they might come and anoint Him” found the tomb empty (Mark 16:1).

witnesses.matthew: Sets the anointing between the leaders’ plot and Judas’s bargain (26:3–16), so a woman’s costly love stands between two acts of calculation. Matthew does not spare the Twelve: he says simply that “His disciples” were indignant.
witnesses.mark: Gives the vivid touches: the broken flask, the price, the sharp criticism, and Jesus’ gentle verdict, “She has done what she could.” Like Matthew, he frames the scene with the plot against Jesus (14:1–11).
witnesses.john: Names Mary, Martha, Lazarus and Judas, and tells what John later knew about Judas and the money box. He dates the supper to the night before the entry and ends with the plot to kill Lazarus, the living proof of Jesus’ last great sign.

seeing.reveals: Jesus accepts lavish worship without embarrassment and speaks calmly of His own burial. He knows He is days from death, and He values love poured out on Him above money saved.
seeing.living: Mary’s gift looked wasteful to people who were counting. Jesus called it “a good work” and said, “She has done what she could.” Give Him what is yours to give while the moment is open, and do not let the critics at the table set the value of love for Him.
seeing.ponder: What costly thing would you pour out for Jesus if no one were watching to call it waste?

preaching.big_idea: What others call waste, Jesus calls a good work done for Him.
outline: A memorial that will not fade (9)
preaching.watch_for: Mark wraps this story inside the plot against Jesus (14:1–2, 10–11). A woman gives something worth a year’s wages for Jesus; one of the Twelve then offers to hand Him over for money. The frame invites the contrast.
